title: About
text:
I am a biostatistician with more than ten years of experience in academia and industry, and I have been programming statistics in R for just as long.

Current role: Biostatistics Scientist in the Field Solutions function at Bayer Crop Science. I design and plan trials, determine sample sizes through simulation, and maintain an automated analysis pipeline. I was the main statistician on a three-year cross-functional project with market development, biologicals and field solutions.
Earlier: postdoctoral researcher at a research institute in Germany, independent statistical consultant, lecturer, and environmental statistics analyst.
Education: Biotechnology Engineering (Universidad de las Fuerzas Armadas ESPE, Ecuador), Master of Statistics with a specialisation in biometrics, including clinical trials (KU Leuven, Belgium), and PhD in Bioinformatics (Jacobs University Bremen, Germany).

title: About
text:
Teaching
In my free time I teach free online statistics courses. The most recent, Bioestadística en R (2025), was a 40-hour workshop for students and researchers in biology and agriculture. It covered R programming, data wrangling with the tidyverse, visualisation with ggplot2, statistical inference, design of experiments, linear and generalized linear models, and reproducible reports with Quarto. Like this site, its materials were built with Quarto and included interactive in-browser exercises.

title: Self-check
text: Nine short questions on the sample session, two or three per learning goal. You get two tries per question, then the answer and an explanation. Anonymous: nothing is stored or sent anywhere.

title: Self-check
text:
Goal 1: Recognising grouped data

1. A researcher records 40 trials from each of 12 macaques and compares two conditions with a t-test on all 480 trials. What is the main problem?
The sample size is too small for a t-test
Trials from the same macaque are not independent, so the standard errors
are too small
A t-test cannot handle 480 observations
Each macaque should be analysed separatelyCheck answer


The 480 trials are not 480 independent pieces of information: trials from the same animal are more alike than trials from different animals. Treating them as independent overstates the evidence (pseudoreplication). A mixed model with a random effect for macaque accounts for this.




2. Which of these datasets is not hierarchical?
Eye-tracking trials recorded from several infants
Vocalisations from individuals living in several social groups
One measurement per lizard, with every lizard from a different mother
Neurons recorded in several sessions from the same monkeysCheck answer


If every lizard has a different mother, there are no clusters: each observation comes from its own “group”. All the other examples have repeated observations within a higher-level unit (infant, social group, session, monkey).

title: Self-check
section: Goal 2: Random intercepts and the ICC
text:
Goal 2: Random intercepts and the ICC

3. In lmer(dors ~ sex + (1 | mother), data = lizard), what does (1 | mother) do?
Adds a separate fixed effect for each mother
Gives each mother her own baseline, drawn from a normal distribution
Removes the variation between mothers from the data
Lets the effect of sex differ between mothersCheck answer


(1 | mother) is a random intercept: each mother gets her own baseline \(\alpha_i \sim N(0, \sigma^2_{mother})\). The model estimates how much mothers vary (\(\sigma^2_{mother}\)) instead of a separate parameter for each one. Letting the effect of sex differ between mothers would be a random slope, (sex | mother).




4. The variance between mothers is 1.78 and the residual variance is 2.25. What is the intraclass correlation (ICC)?
0.79
0.44
0.56
1.26Check answer


\(\rho = \dfrac{\sigma^2_{mother}}{\sigma^2_{mother} + \sigma^2} = \dfrac{1.78}{1.78 + 2.25} = 0.44\). About 44% of the variability in dorsal scales is due to differences between mothers.




5. What does an ICC close to 0 tell you?
Observations from the same cluster are hardly more alike than
observations from different clusters
The model has failed to converge
There is no effect of the predictors
All observations within a cluster are identicalCheck answer


An ICC near 0 means the clusters explain almost none of the variability, so the grouping matters little. An ICC near 1 would mean observations within a cluster are nearly identical. The ICC says nothing about the fixed effects.

title: Self-check
section: Goal 3: Choosing between an LMM and a GLMM
text:
Goal 3: Choosing between an LMM and a GLMM

6. On each of 20 trials, you record whether an infant looked at the target (1) or not (0). Which model fits best?
lmer(looked ~ condition + (1 | infant))
glmer(looked ~ condition + (1 | infant), family = binomial)
glm(looked ~ condition, family = binomial)
lm(looked ~ condition)Check answer


The response is binary, so we need a binomial family with a logit link (a GLM), and the trials are grouped within infants, so we need a random effect (a mixed model). Together: a GLMM. The glm() ignores the grouping; lmer() and lm() assume a continuous, normally distributed response.




7. You count the number of aggressive interactions of each individual per week, over 10 weeks. Which model is the natural starting point?
A Gaussian linear mixed model with a random intercept for individual
A Poisson (or negative binomial) GLMM with a random intercept for
individual
A binomial GLMM with a random intercept for week
A separate t-test for each weekCheck answer


Counts call for a Poisson family with a log link, or a negative binomial if the counts are overdispersed. Repeated weeks from the same individual call for a random intercept for individual.

title: Self-check
text:
Goal 4: Interpreting a GLMM

8. In a logistic GLMM, the estimate for session is 0.50. What does this mean?
For a typical individual, the odds of a correct answer are multiplied by
about 1.65 per session
The probability of a correct answer increases by 0.50 per session
The population-average probability of a correct answer increases by 50%
per session
Half of the individuals improve from one session to the nextCheck answer


Coefficients in a logistic model are on the log-odds scale: \(e^{0.50} \approx 1.65\) is the odds ratio per session. In a GLMM, this is the effect for an individual with random effect \(b_i = 0\), the typical individual, not the population average.




9. Why is the population-average curve flatter than the curve of the typical individual in a logistic GLMM?
Averaging S-shaped curves that are shifted left and right gives a
flatter curve
Because the model is misspecified
Because the sample size is small
Because random effects shrink the fixed effects towards zeroCheck answer


Each individual has its own S-shaped curve, shifted by its random intercept. Averaging these curves at each value of the predictor gives a curve that rises more gently than any single one. In a linear mixed model the two coincide; with a non-linear link such as the logit, they do not.









Want to go further?



The next sessions of Module B3 and B4 cover the hands-on work in R, random slopes and crossed random effects.

title: Sample session
text:
Context

Audience: early-career PhD researchers who have used linear models but have not met mixed models before.
Place in the curriculum: first session of Module B3, Mixed models. It builds on B1 (linear models) and B2 (GLMs).
Length: a 15-minute version for the demonstration; in the course, the same input is followed by about an hour of hands-on work.

title: Sample session
text:
Learning goals
By the end of the session, students will be able to:

Recognise when their data are grouped (repeated trials, siblings, individuals in social groups) and why that breaks the independence assumption.
Explain what a random intercept is and what the intraclass correlation tells them.
Choose between a linear mixed model and a GLMM based on the type of their response.
Interpret the coefficients of a GLMM as effects for the typical individual.

After the input, students:

title: Curriculum
text:
Format

Track A runs as a compact bootcamp at the start of each semester (four sessions), so new PhD researchers are ready for Track B.
Track B runs weekly over a semester. Modules B1 to B3 build on each other; B4 and B5 can be taken independently once B3 is done.
Track C consists of two workshops, followed by individual consulting on each student’s own manuscript.
Each session combines a short conceptual input (about 30 to 45 minutes) with hands-on work in R, ideally on the students’ own data.
Language: English. All materials are openly available on this site and on GitHub.

The table for each track below shows how learning outcomes, activities and assessment are aligned.

title: Curriculum
text:
Capstone: a reproducible mini-paper
The programme ends with a short, reproducible report on the student’s own data: a methods and results section with figures and tables, rendered from code. Students discuss it in an individual consulting appointment. Because this assessment mirrors what they need for their thesis, it rewards exactly the skills the course is meant to build.

title: Curriculum
text:
How the programme connects

Consulting: recurring questions from consulting turn into new short workshops or FAQ entries.
Existing courses: Track A and B1 build on, and can be coordinated with, the statistics courses already offered in the biology and psychology programmes.
Graduate schools: modules could be offered as credited courses in the graduate programmes, to be agreed with the programme coordinators.

title: Teaching approach
text: Every session starts from what students should be able to do afterwards, and the activities and checks are built around that (constructive alignment). In the sample session, each of the four learning goals is practised in the lecture and checked again in the self-check.

title: Teaching approach
text: Every session starts from what students should be able to do afterwards, and the activities and checks are built around that (constructive alignment). In the sample session, each of the four learning goals is practised in the lecture and checked again in the self-check.

title: Teaching approach
section: 2. Concepts before code, plots before models
text:
2. Concepts before code, plots before models
Students first understand why a method is needed, then how to run it in R. Every modelling session starts with a plot of the raw data. In the sample session, a plot of lizards grouped by their mothers makes the need for a mixed model obvious before any equation appears.

title: Teaching approach
text:
3. Students’ own data
From the second session on, students apply each method to their own project, or to a close match when their data are not ready yet. This makes the content immediately useful and reveals the real problems (messy exports, unbalanced designs, convergence issues) that textbook data hide.

title: Teaching approach
text:
4. Active learning
Short inputs alternate with hands-on work. Typical formats:

Think-pair-share: “What do you notice in this plot?” before revealing the answer.
Live coding: students code along; mistakes are made, and fixed, in public.
Pair programming in the data-skills track.
Model clinics: students present their model and get feedback from peers and the instructor.

title: Teaching approach
text:
5. A mixed audience by design
CBB researchers arrive with very different backgrounds in statistics and programming. The programme handles this by:

Modular entry: a short entry self-check tells students which data-skills modules they can skip.
Examples from all CBB fields: looking-time data, primate field observations, neural recordings, tracking data.
Several routes to the same content: slides, worked code, interactive exercises and recordings.

How students prefer to learn is partly shaped by the learning environment (the outer layer of Curry’s onion model). Varied formats and well-designed activities are therefore not decoration: they change how students engage.

title: Teaching approach
text:
6. Feedback throughout, assessment that matters

Formative: anonymous self-checks with explanations after each session, and peer feedback on figures and models.
Summative: a reproducible mini-paper on the student’s own data (see the curriculum).

What is assessed drives what is learned. Assessing a realistic analysis of their own data pushes students towards the skills they will actually use.

title: Teaching approach
text:
7. Open and reproducible materials
All slides, code and exercises are written in Quarto and R, version-controlled and openly available. The materials themselves model the reproducible practice the course teaches.

title: Teaching approach
text:
8. Improving the teaching

A one-minute feedback form at the end of each session (“What was clearest? What was muddiest?”).
Self-check results show which concepts need another pass.
Questions from consulting reveal gaps in the curriculum and lead to new short workshops.

title: Exercises
text: These exercises follow the sample session step by step. The code runs in your browser: no installation needed. Type your code in the boxes and press Run Code. Stuck? Open the Hint tab, and compare your answer with the Solution tab.

title: Exercises
section: Part 1: Look at the data first
text:
Part 1: Look at the data first

Exercise 1.1: How is the data grouped?
How many lizards and how many mothers are in lizard? Fill in the blanks.

ExerciseHintSolution













nrow() counts the rows of a data frame. n_distinct() from dplyr counts the different values in a column. Which column identifies the mothers?




nrow(lizard)
n_distinct(lizard$mother)
102 lizards from 29 mothers: on average about 3.5 siblings per mother.






Exercise 1.2: Plot before you model
Complete the code to plot the number of dorsal scales for each mother, coloured by sex. What do you notice?

ExerciseHintSolution













The x-axis shows the grouping (mother), the y-axis the response (dors), and the colour the predictor of interest (sex).




ggplot(lizard, aes(x = mother, y = dors, colour = sex)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5, alpha = 0.8) +
  labs(x = "Mother", y = "Dorsal scales") +
  theme_minimal()
Mothers differ a lot in their typical number of scales, and within a mother, males tend to have more scales than females. Siblings are more alike than unrelated lizards.

title: Exercises
text:
Part 2: Accounting for the grouping

Exercise 2.1: Ignoring the mothers
Compare males and females with a two-sample t-test that assumes equal variances. Is there evidence of a difference?

ExerciseHintSolution













Use t.test() with a formula response ~ group, the data argument and var.equal = TRUE.




t.test(dors ~ sex, data = lizard, var.equal = TRUE)
\(p \approx 0.10\): no clear evidence of a difference. But the test treats all 102 lizards as independent (df = 100), which they are not.






Exercise 2.2: Your first linear mixed model
Fit a linear mixed model for dors with sex as a fixed effect and a random intercept for mother. Then compare the sex effect with the one from lm(dors ~ sex).

ExerciseHintSolution













A random intercept for mother is written (1 | mother) and added to the formula like any other term: dors ~ sex + (1 | mother).




fit_lm  <- lm(dors ~ sex, data = lizard)
fit_lmm <- lmer(dors ~ sex + (1 | mother), data = lizard)

summary(fit_lm)$coefficients
summary(fit_lmm)$coefficients
The mixed model compares lizards within mothers: the sex effect becomes larger (about \(-0.83\) scales for females) and its standard error smaller, so the t value is now about \(-2.6\).
Note that lme4 does not print p-values. The lmerTest package adds them, as in the slides.






Exercise 2.3: How alike are siblings?
Extract the variance components from fit_lmm and compute the intraclass correlation (ICC).

ExerciseHintSolution













The ICC is the share of the total variance that lies between mothers: \[\rho = \frac{\sigma^2_{mother}}{\sigma^2_{mother} + \sigma^2}\]




fit_lmm <- lmer(dors ~ sex + (1 | mother), data = lizard)

vc <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(fit_lmm))
s2_mother   <- vc$vcov[vc$grp == "mother"]
s2_residual <- vc$vcov[vc$grp == "Residual"]

icc <- s2_mother / (s2_mother + s2_residual)
icc
\(\rho \approx 1.78 / (1.78 + 2.25) = 0.44\): about 44% of the variability in dorsal scales is due to the mother.

title: Exercises
section: Part 3: When the response is binary
text:
Part 3: When the response is binary

Exercise 3.1: Plot the learning curves
Compute the proportion of correct answers for each individual and session, then plot one line per individual.

ExerciseHintSolution













We want one proportion per individual (id) and session (session), and one line per individual.




learn_sum <- learn |>
  group_by(id, session) |>
  summarise(p = mean(correct), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(learn_sum, aes(x = session, y = p, group = id)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(x = "Session", y = "Proportion correct") +
  theme_minimal()
All individuals tend to improve, but they start at very different levels: another sign of grouped data.






Exercise 3.2: Fit a GLMM
Fit a logistic GLMM for correct with session as a fixed effect and a random intercept for id. Then compute the odds ratio per session.

ExerciseHintSolution













The formula is built just like in lmer(): correct ~ session + (1 | id). For a binary response, use family = binomial.




fit_glmm <- glmer(correct ~ session + (1 | id), family = binomial, data = learn)

summary(fit_glmm)

exp(fixef(fit_glmm))
The estimate for session is on the log-odds scale. exp() turns it into an odds ratio: for a typical individual, the odds of a correct answer are multiplied by this factor in each session. The Std.Dev. of id under Random effects shows how much individuals differ.






Exercise 3.3: Challenge: typical individual or population average?
Using fit_glmm, compute the probability of a correct answer in session 8 (a) for a typical individual (\(b_i = 0\)) and (b) averaged over the population of individuals. Why do they differ?

ExerciseHintSolution













Add each simulated random intercept b_draw to the linear predictor, transform with plogis(), and take the mean() of the resulting probabilities.




fit_glmm <- glmer(correct ~ session + (1 | id), family = binomial, data = learn)
beta <- fixef(fit_glmm)
sd_b <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(fit_glmm))$sdcor[1]

p_typical <- plogis(beta[1] + beta[2] * 8)

b_draw <- rnorm(10000, mean = 0, sd = sd_b)
p_average <- mean(plogis(beta[1] + beta[2] * 8 + b_draw))

c(typical = p_typical, average = p_average)
The population average is closer to 50% than the typical individual. Averaging S-shaped curves that are shifted left and right gives a flatter curve: in a GLMM, the fixed effects describe the typical individual, not the population average.

text:

title: Statistical consulting
text: Teaching and consulting are two sides of the same service. Courses give everyone a common foundation; consulting helps with the specific questions of each project.

title: Statistical consulting
text:
What consulting covers

Study design and sample size: before data collection, including simulation-based power analysis and preregistration.
Analysis: choosing, fitting and checking models for the data at hand.
Interpretation and reporting: what the results mean and how to present them.
Reviewer comments: responding to statistical questions from journals.
Grant applications: statistical sections, power analyses and data management plans.

title: Statistical consulting
text:
How it works

Short request: a brief description of the research question, design, data and timeline, so the first meeting starts well prepared.
First meeting (about 45 minutes): we clarify the question, look at the data together and agree on next steps.
Follow-up: further meetings as needed, plus weekly open drop-in hours for quick questions.







The earlier, the better



The most valuable consulting happens before data are collected. A short conversation about design and sample size can save months of work later.

title: Statistical consulting
text:
Principles

Guide, don’t take over. The aim is that researchers understand and can defend their own analysis.
Questions first, methods second. We start from the scientific question, not from a statistical test.
Reproducible from the start. Analyses are set up as scripts or Quarto documents that others can rerun.
Fair credit. Substantial statistical contributions are acknowledged according to the usual authorship guidelines.

title: Statistical consulting
text:
Feeding back into teaching
Questions that come up again and again in consulting become new FAQ entries, examples in the courses, or short focused workshops. In this way the curriculum keeps up with what CBB researchers actually need.

title: Statistics and Data Science Training for CBB
text:
PhD researchers in CBB come from psychology, behavioural and cognitive biology, systems neuroscience and data science. They collect very different data, from infant eye-tracking and primate field observations to neural recordings and video tracking, but they share the same journey: get the data in shape, model it honestly, and publish it.
This site describes a modular training programme built around that journey, and how it connects to statistical consulting.

title: Statistics and Data Science Training for CBB
text:
Three tracks, one path



A. Data skills
R programming, data wrangling, exploration and visualisation, and reproducible workflows. Modular: students skip what they already master.




B. Statistical modelling
From linear models to GLMs and mixed models, plus study design and simulation-based power analysis.




C. From analysis to publication
Reporting statistics, publication-ready figures and tables, reproducible manuscripts and open science.



See the full curriculum →

title: Statistics and Data Science Training for CBB
text:
Guiding principles

Concepts before code, plots before models. Every modelling session starts with a picture of the data.
Your own data. From the second session on, students work on their own projects.
Active learning. Short inputs, then hands-on work, discussion and feedback.
Aligned outcomes, activities and assessment. Each session states what students will be able to do, and checks it.
Open and reproducible. All materials, code and data examples are openly available.
